# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 11 (Bu-Vb Pc11)

**ID:** Bu-Vb Pc11
**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 11
**Title (English, from literature):** Destroying plants
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m1.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 11 (PTS Vin IV 34) formulates the monastic rule prohibiting the intentional destruction of plant life (*bhūtagāmapātavyatāya pācittiyam*), stipulating that a monk who damages vegetation commits an offense requiring expiation (*pācittiya*) [Bechert 1992; Schmithausen 2009]. In the canonical word analysis (*padabhājanīya*), *bhūtagāma* ("vegetative growth") is defined via five modes of propagation (*pañca bījajātāni*): plants generated from roots (*mūlabīja*), stems (*khandhabīja*), joints (*phalubīja*), cuttings (*aggabīja*), and seeds (*bījabīja*) [Clarke, Pārājika]. The archaic term *pātavyatā* has been analyzed by scholars as denoting uncontrolled or ruthless behavior toward plants [Schmithausen 2009]. In the origin narrative, the rule is motivated by public reproach: householders complained that cutting trees harmed living beings endowed with one sense-faculty (*ekindriyaṁ jīva*) or destroyed the abodes of tree deities (*devatā*) [Deutsch and Bontekoe 1999; Bechert 1992; Schmithausen 1991; Schmithausen 2009]. In later ethical and legal analysis, destroying vegetation—such as plucking flowers with devotion to honor the Triple Gem—is classified as an infraction of institutional monastic convention (*paṇṇattivajja*) rather than an intrinsically unwholesome act (*lokavajja*) [Entrance to the Vinaya 1969; Keown 1992].

 Whereas the Pali Pātimokkha rule refers strictly to plants (*bhūtagāma*), many parallels across other schools and standard Suttapiṭaka formulas (such as the *Dīgha Nikāya* stock description *bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambha*) explicitly prohibit injuring both seeds and plants [Buddhism into the Year 2000; Bechert 1992; Schmithausen 2009]. The Pali and Dharmaguptaka traditions uniquely place this rule immediately after the prohibition against digging soil (Pācittiya 10), reflecting a shared thematic cluster [Schmithausen 1991].

**Sources**

- [Buddhism into the Year 2000] Buddhism into the Year 2000: International Conference Proceedings (1999) — Discussed the divergence between the Pātimokkha phrasing and the combined seeds-and-plants phrasing in Sutta passages and other Vinayas.
- [Clarke, Pārājika] Shayne Clarke, Pārājika: The Myth of Permanent and Irrevocable Expulsion from the Buddhist Order — Provided the canonical definition of bhūtagāma as five kinds of propagation and noted the Chinese Mūlasarvāstivādin parallel.
- [Deutsch and Bontekoe 1999] Eliot Deutsch and Ron Bontekoe, A Companion to World Philosophies (1999) — Discussed the rationale of the rule regarding non-Buddhist views of plant life and lay criticism.
- [Bechert 1992] Heinz Bechert (ed.), The Dating of the Historical Buddha, Part 2 (1992) [incorporating paper by L. Schmithausen] — Cited the Pali rule formula and analyzed the justification grounded in popular belief in the sentience of plants.
- [Entrance to the Vinaya 1969] Vinayamukha: Entrance to the Vinaya, Vol. 1 (1969) — Explained the categorization of plant destruction under paṇṇattivajja.
- [Keown 1992] Damien Keown, The Nature of Buddhist Ethics (1992) — Noted the connection between Pācittiya 11 and the ethical distinction between lokavajja and paṇṇattivajja.
- [Schmithausen 2009] Lambert Schmithausen, Plants in Early Buddhism and the Far Eastern Idea of the Buddha-Nature of Grasses and Trees (2009) — Analyzed the archaic term pātavyatā, the notion of ekindriyaṁ jīva, and comparative Vinaya readings.
- [Schmithausen 1991] Lambert Schmithausen, The Problem of the Sentience of Plants in Earliest Buddhism (1991) — Discussed the etymology of bhūtagāma, the tree deity story, and structural placement alongside digging earth.
